answers.answer:
Saturday's yours, so protect the café slot first — that's where the words actually come from. Get down there before 8 for a long stretch, aim to beat your 2200, then take a real break and decide at lunch whether a second sitting is worth it.

Keep the rest of the day loose. Planning the whole thing hour by hour usually turns into planning instead of writing.

One thing worth trying: pick the spot you'll stop at *before* you start, so Sunday has an easy entry point instead of a blank page.

answers.answer:
The honest answer: don't plan a writing day, plan a morning. Every time the words have actually come, it's been the before-breakfast slot at the café — 1800 words on chapter 4, 2200 on chapter 5. An all-day Saturday has never been the thing that produces pages; the evening hours never have, and a wide-open day tends to turn into one.

So protect the morning: café, before it opens, phone away, one block, no errands first. Then leave the rest of Saturday free without expecting it to be more writing.

One thing worth naming — the monitor is also racing the December trip, and it's the same hours you'd be spending. Do you want Saturday's morning to go to the book, or split it?

Saturday's a great shot. My honest take: don't plan the whole day around writing — plan the morning around it, and let the rest be whatever.

The café slot is where the book actually moves: chapter 4 went 1800 words to done there, and Sep 13's 2200 was your biggest morning yet. So treat Saturday like a normal café morning, just without needing to leave for anything afterward. Wake, go down, write until you're dry. That alone could be a big day.

One thing to weigh: the plant monitor has a December deadline too, and mornings are the only hours the book has ever used. So if you want the monitor to move at all, give it the afternoon — one unbroken stretch, not squeezed around writing.

What I'd avoid is scheduling an evening writing session as a "second push." You've gone back to that hour repeatedly and it's never produced anything usable. A free day tempts you into a full writing day, but your own record says the morning carries it.

probes.ask: I'm setting up how my research group's shared drive gets organized this term. Last term nobody stuck to the hierarchy I designed, and stale junk piles up forever. How should I approach it this time?
points: Suggests letting the structure come from how people actually save and look for files, formalizing the patterns that emerge, like the campus paths paved where students actually walked
Suggests letting files that nobody touches fade away or get archived automatically over time, like the ant colony's scent evaporating from unused routes
Explicitly connects the advice to something Shreyas talked about before (the ant colonies or the campus desire lines)

answers.answer:
Last time the problem wasn't the hierarchy itself, it's that nothing enforced it and nothing removed old stuff. So this term, pick two or three rules people will actually follow — like one folder per project, named by who owns it and when it ends — and make cleanup automatic rather than a chore. For example, anything untouched for a set time gets flagged or auto-moved to an archive. And say the rules out loud at the start, once, so it's a group agreement and not your personal preference.

What's the drive actually for — active working files, or is it also the long-term archive? That changes how aggressive the cleanup should be.

And give junk an expiry instead of a rule against it. A scratch area that auto-deletes after 30 days makes stale piling impossible, and people stop defending their mess.

Worth first asking why they ignored it last term. My guess, not something you've told me: the hierarchy was built for filing, not for finding, so their path of least resistance went around it.

answers.answer:
You already know the answer to this one — you told it to me about the campus path: the planned layout always loses to where feet actually go. Last term your hierarchy was the architect's drawing, and your group's filing was the desire line.

So don't redesign the tree from scratch. Start by looking at where files actually landed last term and how people searched for them. Then make that the structure, rather than fighting it.

For the stale-junk half — that's the dish problem. Nobody cleans an unnamed shared pile because it's never anyone's turn. One name, one folder, one deadline, and it stops being a negotiation. A rotating owner per folder who prunes it on a set date will do more than any taxonomy.

One practical wrinkle: search often beats folders for a research group, so don't over-invest in a perfect hierarchy if everyone just types a filename into the search box. Watch the feet before you pour the concrete.

So don't design the folder tree first. Watch where files actually land for a week or two, then make those the real folders. The structure that matches how people already work is the one that survives.

For the stale junk: that's the no-owner problem, like the dishes. A shared drive with no one responsible for tidying is everyone's and no one's. Either give it a rule that runs itself — auto-archive anything untouched for a year, say — or the cleanup depends on someone deciding every time, which is exactly what fails. answers.answer:
You already know the answer, because you told it to me on the campus path: the planned layout always loses to where feet actually go. Your hierarchy was the drawn path, and last term everyone walked the short way — that's not a discipline problem, it's data.

So this time, don't design the tree first. Watch where files actually get put for a week or two, then harden whatever spots people already reach for. And for the stale junk: don't rely on anyone deciding to clean up. Set a rule that fires on its own — anything untouched for six months archives itself. Same move as the dish captain and the pheromone fading: the arrangement carries the behavior, nobody has to decide in the moment.

One thing worth being honest about, from your own habits: the forty tabs and the always-on WiFi say you won't prune it by hand either. So the cleanup has to be automatic from day one, or it won't happen at all.

This weekend? Block a late-night stretch, not a morning one. Your two biggest sessions ever were after midnight — 3000 and then 2500 — and the second one you actually chose, so it isn't just insomnia luck.

That said, the thing that made both work was the same thing the café gives you: one long unbroken stretch with nothing else in it. So pick whichever night you can keep completely empty and stay up for, and treat the café mornings as the backup.

One caution: you've got the plant monitor and the December trip both eating mornings too, so if the weekend mornings are for the build, the night slot is the one that won't cost you anything.

Chapter 5. No count reported since the 13th, and the café mornings are the only place it moves. Two weeks without them is two weeks of nothing.

Here's a shape for the next eight weeks, built around what actually works for you.

Mornings at the café stay theirs: before-breakfast, no clock, one thing only. Alternate chapter 5 and the monitor rather than splitting a morning — chapter 5 Mon/Wed/Fri, monitor Tue/Thu/Sat. Sunday morning stays empty or it becomes the spillover.

The half marathon needs three runs a week, not five. Tue/Thu/Sat, 30 to 45 minutes, easy pace, building the long one on Saturday. Do not put runs in the café slot — running is the one thing you've never enjoyed, so it gets its own time after breakfast or in the evening.

Evenings are for nothing that matters. If chapter 5 wants a midnight stretch, take it, but don't plan it.

The monitor should be finished and sitting on the windowsill by mid-November, before the race eats your weekends.

One caveat: I'm sketching this from what usually happens for you, not from what you told me this week. If the last few days have gone differently, tell me and I'll redo it.

Here's what I'd actually build it around: you only have one real work slot, the before-breakfast café stretch, and you've got three things fighting for it. So the routine has to split that slot by day rather than try to do all three every morning.

Here's the sketch for late Sept through mid-Nov:

Monday, Wednesday, Friday: café slot is writing. Chapter 5, same as always, same place.

Tuesday, Thursday: café slot is the monitor build. You're at the firmware stage now, so these are the mornings for the loop and the battery stuff.

Saturday: café slot is the long run, building up week by week. Sunday: rest, or an easy short one.

Two short runs midweek, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, 30 min, no clock-watching — just miles.

Everything else stays as it is. One thing per slot, no negotiating in the moment.

Past Nov 15: drop the running, hand that slot back to the monitor, and give the last weeks before December entirely to the rig so it's actually running itself when you leave.

Want me to tighten the run build-up into actual weekly distances?

synthesis.answer:
Two things are fighting in that sentence, and last term the design lost. The hierarchy was a plan; where people actually drop files is the desire path. So don't design harder, watch first.

For a week, note where files land and what gets duplicated. Then set the condition instead of the rule: a folder that's obvious from the filename alone, auto-archive anything untouched for a term, and one clearly-named dumping ground so "stale junk" has a place to go instead of everywhere.

And stale stuff doesn't need a human deciding to delete it—like the ant scent fading, unused things can expire on their own. Want me to sketch the actual folder tree?

I can, but let me not just hand you a generic timetable. The useful thing here is to build it around what your own memory says actually works, and against what never has.

What I'd anchor it on:
Mornings at the café before 8 are your proven writing slot — that's where chapter 4 finished. Two midnight sessions in a row worked too, but two isn't a pattern, and stacking night writing on top of early mornings is the one way to break the thing that's carrying chapter 5.

So the shape I'd suggest: writing five mornings a week, café, before it opens. Chapter 5 keeps the slot that already works.

Plant monitor: one evening a week, since you just closed out the drift with the water calibration. Next real step is the siphoning fix on the watering rig — check valve, or outlet above the water line.
The flat: the dish captain already runs itself, so nothing to schedule there. It's working.
Ideas like the parking and gym refund: one block a week to write them up properly if you want them to go anywhere.

Two questions before I make it concrete. How many waking hours do you realistically have outside work, and do you want the midnight slot in there at all, or should that stay something you only use when it offers itself?
